strengths: Clear and elegant theoretical motivation showing that optimal policy π* can inherit biases from reference policy πSFT due to KL regularization (Equation 6)
Simple and practical method requiring no additional training, using only the log-likelihood ratio between DPO and SFT models
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 diverse datasets, multiple model families/scales, with consistent improvements (Table 1: win rates 0.70-0.93)
Strong empirical results with substantial improvements over baselines (e.g., Agrilla/Llama 3B: 5.64 vs 4.54 for EFT, 3.02 for Best-of-2)
Thoughtful engineering including min-α filtering to prevent over-optimization and entropy thresholding for beam search stability
Practical extensions demonstrated via iterative DPO showing near full-data performance with only 10% of preference data
Evaluation with both internal oracle models and external reward models (Skywork, Nectar) strengthens generalization claims
Good reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, multiple datasets, and code availability
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification: while Equation 6 motivates the problem, no formal proof that log-likelihood ratio is optimal token reward or that token-level optimization improves sequence-level alignment

Significant discrepancy between oracle reward improvements (Table 1: 0.78-0.93 win rates) and AlpacaEval results (Table 2: 0.44-0.82), raising questions about generalization and oracle reward validity
Evaluation setup biases comparisons: oracle models trained on 100% data while DPO uses 10%, and the 90/10→10% subsampling creates an artificial regime
Insufficient hyperparameter analysis: α=0.1 and entropy threshold τ are fixed without ablation or guidance for practitioners; no sensitivity studies across datasets
Computational cost inadequately addressed: requires 2 forward passes per token but only mentioned in limitations; no detailed wall-clock comparisons despite being critical for practitioners
Limited novelty: core idea of log-likelihood ratios applies DPO theory and builds on contrastive decoding (Li et al., 2023a) without significant conceptual advance
Incomplete failure analysis: all qualitative examples show positive cases; no discussion of failure modes, degraded outputs, or when AAD underperforms
Iterative DPO results concerning: win rate drops from 72.8% to 57.3% across iterations (Figure 7), suggesting advantages partly stem from initial DPO quality rather than fundamental superiority
Beam search treatment underdeveloped: entropy thresholding (Section 6, Figure 6) is important but lacks explanation of why it helps; appears as methodological addition deserving more analysis
Missing comparisons with recent work including ORPO (Hong et al., 2024) and other inference-time alignment methods

strengths: Clear motivation grounded in theoretical observation that π* inherits SFT biases (Eq. 6)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 datasets, multiple model scales, and both internal/external oracles
Consistent and often substantial empirical improvements in oracle reward across diverse settings
Simple, practical method requiring no auxiliary models beyond existing DPO setup
Practical contribution of iterative DPO for data-constrained alignment scenarios
Thorough appendices with training details supporting reproducibility
Effective qualitative analysis showing AAD's semantic advantages over greedy/BoN baselines
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core approach is near-identical to contrastive decoding (Li et al. 2023a) with min-alpha filtering directly borrowed; relationship to EFT (Mitchell et al. 2024) insufficiently differentiated
Incomplete theoretical justification: no proof that token-level log-ratio maximization optimizes sequence-level alignment; greedy approximation not analyzed
Experimental design bias: 10%/90% picker/oracle split disadvantages BoN-picker while AAD also uses 10% data; BoN-oracle uses 10x more data yet is used for both selection and evaluation
Computational cost claims unsupported: paper claims 'compute-equivalent' to BoN but AAD requires 2 forward passes per token; no wall-clock timing provided
Method fragility understated: Figure 6 shows rapid degradation without entropy thresholding, suggesting unreliable token-level rewards; requires careful tuning of multiple hyperparameters (α, τ)
Incomplete related work coverage: missing experimental comparisons with energy-based decoding, DeAl, ARGS, and other recent inference-time methods mentioned in paper
Mixed external evaluation results: AlpacaEval (Table 2) shows modest and inconsistent improvements compared to strong claims in main text
Practical constraints understated: requires both SFT and DPO models in memory/accessible; applicability limited to DPO specifically
Iterative DPO lacks rigor: unclear if improvements come from AAD generation quality vs. data augmentation; procedure underspecified; no comparison to alternative synthetic data methods
Missing ablations: α parameter chosen as 0.1 without ablation or justification; entropy threshold τ selection not explained; no sensitivity analyses
No statistical significance testing: win rates reported without confidence intervals or multiple-testing correction; some absolute improvements are modest
Reproducibility concerns: code link not provided in A.6 despite claims; model naming inconsistencies; hyperparameter choices not justified
Limited scope: only tested on alignment tasks; generalization to general generation or other preference optimization methods (IPO, KTO) unknown; only English results

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical foundation: Clear insight (Eq. 6) that optimal DPO policy inherits SFT biases, grounded in prior work showing DPO learns a Q-function
Simple and practical method: No additional training required, uses only log-likelihood ratios of existing models, straightforward to implement

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Consistent improvements across 6 datasets and 4 model scales, thorough ablations on β-sensitivity, data scarcity, beam search, and external AlpacaEval validation
Competitive with best-of-N: Matches oracle-guided beam search despite oracle having 10x more training data (Fig. 2), demonstrating efficiency
Practical secondary contribution: Iterative DPO application addresses data scarcity, approaching full-dataset performance with 10% of data
Robustness across settings: Consistent gains across diverse benchmark datasets, model families, and hyperparameter regimes
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-organized paper with intuitive figures, comprehensive training details in appendix, and code to be released
weaknesses: Imprecise theoretical framing: Claims of 'implicit reward optimization' are somewhat loose—the method performs straightforward greedy maximization of token ratios, not true implicit optimization. Gap between token-level greedy maximization and sequence-level reward maximization not rigorously justified
Ad-hoc design choices: α=0.1 filtering threshold appears arbitrary with limited ablation; entropy thresholding (Section 6) presented as empirical fix rather than principled approach
Practical constraints limit applicability: Requires access to both SFT and DPO models (excludes proprietary models), 2x inference-time compute cost, limited to DPO-only alignment

Discrepancy between internal and external evaluations: Very high win rates on internal benchmarks (0.9+) raise calibration concerns; AlpacaEval shows much more modest improvements (0.73-0.80), suggesting results may be metric/dataset dependent
Limited method understanding: No systematic error analysis or failure mode discussion; unclear which completion types benefit most from AAD; qualitative examples appear cherry-picked
Iterative DPO feels orthogonal: While interesting, Section 6 reads as a separate application rather than integral to core AAD contribution

Insufficient technical details: How exactly is oracle reward computed? Why do picker accuracies vary so widely (62.4%-93%, Table 3) and what's the impact? Relationship to contrastive decoding could be clearer

strengths: Comprehensive empirical validation across 6 diverse datasets, multiple model scales (0.6B-13B), and multiple evaluation approaches including external oracles, human evaluation (Table 5), and AlpacaEval
Solid theoretical grounding connecting to DPO-as-Q-function learning with clear mathematical derivation explaining why π* can prefer lower-reward completions
Consistent and substantial improvements in oracle rewards and win rates (Tables 1, 4) demonstrating robustness across different preference datasets and model families
Practical applicability: requires no additional training beyond standard DPO setup; α=0.1 hyperparameter transfers uniformly across all tested settings
Strong reproducibility: detailed training configurations (Section A.3), promised code release, clear dataset references, and ablation studies (Figures 3-5, 9)
Useful additional contribution: iterative DPO with AAD-generated synthetic data nearly closes performance gap with full-dataset training using only 10% of data (Figure 6)
Thorough experimental design with proper comparisons including compute-equivalent conditions and Best-of-N analysis showing favorable efficiency (Figure 2)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution of using log probability ratios as token-level scores is relatively straightforward application of existing techniques (contrastive decoding, EFT); distinction from EFT (which also uses SFT/DPO ratio) could be clearer

Restricted applicability: method only works well with DPO-trained models (explicitly acknowledged limitation); Table 10 shows mixed/poor results with PPO, substantially limiting generality beyond the SFT+DPO pipeline

Significant computational overhead: requires 2x forward passes per token, resulting in ~0.5× throughput of greedy decoding on single GPU; this overhead is largely equivalent to Bo2 sampling, not clearly superior

Moderate reliance on reward model evaluation despite mitigations: AlpacaEval results (Table 2) are less impressive than oracle scores, suggesting possible reward hacking; human evaluation limited to single dataset (3B Llama on Skywork with 502 judgments)
Requires access to original SFT model (not always available for proprietary models), limiting practical deployment in many real-world scenarios

Incomplete analysis of design decisions: why does AAD substantially outperform EFT when both use identical model pair? Min-α filtering borrowed from contrastive decoding but motivation and interaction with main algorithm underexplored
Limited failure mode analysis and discussion of edge cases: qualitative examples are somewhat cherry-picked; no analysis of when/why method fails or sensitivity to misaligned reward models
Experimental setup asymmetry: 90/10 data split means oracle trained on 10x more data than DPO model, though BoN-Oracle comparison partly mitigates this concern

Missing comparisons with concurrent inference-time methods: no comparison with energy-based decoding (Yuan et al. 2025), value-guided search (Liu et al. 2024e), DeAl, or other recent approaches mentioned in related work
Greedy token-level optimization doesn't guarantee sequence-level reward maximization; theoretical gap between MDP formulation and practical algorithm deserves deeper analysis

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 6 datasets, multiple model families, and model scales with consistent improvements
Simple, practical method requiring no additional training and using only existing models (πDPO and πSFT)
Hyperparameter α=0.1 transfers across all datasets without per-dataset tuning, improving practical deployment
Demonstrates practical value through iterative DPO for data-constrained settings
Human evaluation (Table 5) validates that gains extend beyond reward-model evaluation
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core technique (log-likelihood ratio scoring) is borrowed from contrastive decoding (Li et al., 2023b); contribution reduces to applying contrastive decoding to DPO models with α-filtering

Weak theoretical justification: Section A.1 lacks rigorous argument for why token-level greedy maximization should optimize sequence-level alignment; leap from Equation (18) to Algorithm 1 is unjustified
Significant practical limitations understated: 2× computational cost (0.5× greedy throughput), requires SFT model access, fails with PPO models (Table 10), yet these are relegated to brief discussion

Unfair evaluation comparisons: Claims compute-equivalence with BoN despite parallel vs. sequential generation having different latency/memory profiles; imperfect oracle models (70-93% accuracy) lack sensitivity analysis
Weak external evaluation: AlpacaEval results (Table 2) show minimal improvement over baselines, contradicting main claims and warranting deeper investigation
Beam search instability (Figure 7, Section A.4): Naive beam search degrades rapidly and requires entropy thresholding to stabilize, suggesting fundamental issues with the token-level scoring function

Incomplete analysis: No explanation for 8.7× performance variation across datasets (e.g., Skywork vs. Ultrafeedback in Table 1); claims about 'underutilized alignment signal' are vague; no statistical significance testing

Hyperparameter α lacks principled justification: While α=0.1 works empirically, why this value transfers universally across model scales, architectures, and datasets is unexplained; appears to be fortunate coincidence rather than principled design
Missing comparisons: Related work mentions DeAL, ARGS, DeRa, Amulet but provides no empirical comparisons to these inference-time alignment methods
Iterative DPO concerns: Gains are somewhat circular (using better decoder to generate training data); Iter 2 degradation (Table 9) suggests saturation; not a sustainable improvement mechanism

strengths: Strong empirical results across diverse settings: 6 datasets, 4 model scales, 2 model families with consistent 2-3× improvements over baselines and win rates >75%
Comprehensive evaluation combining multiple protocols (oracle rewards, AlpacaEval, external reward models, human evaluation with Elo 1610.1) that validate gains beyond single metrics
Solid theoretical grounding connecting DPO training to Q-function learning with well-articulated MDP framework and token-level advantage function justification
Practical simplicity requiring no specialized training, straightforward implementation, and effectiveness in data-scarce regimes enabling iterative DPO
Thorough experimental methodology with proper compute-equivalent baselines, extensive ablations (α, data scaling, β, overtraining), and reproducibility details including full training specifications
Strong qualitative demonstrations showing improved contextual appropriateness, detail preservation, and fluency compared to greedy and best-of-N baselines
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core technique (log-likelihood ratios with filtering) extends existing ideas from contrastive decoding; contribution is primarily engineering application to DPO rather than fundamental methodological advance

Severely restricted applicability: method only works with DPO pipeline; Table 10 shows 'mixed results' with PPO because it 'does not preserve the SFT-DPO probability gap,' eliminating compatibility with widely-used RLHF/PPO approaches and other recent methods (KTO, ORPO)

Insufficient theoretical justification for design choices: min-α filtering lacks principled analysis versus alternatives; α=0.1 appears dataset-dependent (Figure 3 shows 0.1-0.2 range); claim that log-ratio 'provides more direct way to maximize reward' needs rigorous justification

Significant computational overhead of 2 forward passes per token yielding ~0.5× greedy throughput, limiting practical deployment despite comparable cost to EFT/Bo2; no exploration of efficiency improvements
Requires access to original π_SFT model with no analysis of sensitivity to model mismatch or domain shift, limiting applicability to proprietary settings and failing gracefully

Limited investigation of failure modes: PPO incompatibility (Table 10) minimally explored; AlpacaEval results (Table 2) less conclusive than reward-model evaluation without explanation; iterative DPO saturation (Figure 6) occurs after 1 iteration without investigation of selective data strategies
Comparison with EFT inadequately analyzed despite similar core mechanisms; unclear why AAD substantially outperforms when both use log-likelihood ratios and reference models
Human evaluation limited to single dataset (Skywork) on 3B model with 502 total judgments across 40 raters; unclear prompt/judgment distribution and generalization to other settings
